messages.subject: GP experiment
parts: I wanted to do the leukemia GP survival model in BDA3 with Stan, and first started experimenting with the following simpler GP classification model, which also shows how I would like to define GPs by combining basic covariance functions. With 250 data points Stan gives high N_eff, but sampling is very slow (N_eff/s<1.7e-02 and 5.5 hours to get total of 200 saved iterations from 4 chains (for comparison MML estimate with GPstuff takes less than 1.5s)). With 1000 data points I run out of memory in my laptop (using top, I can see the process going over 5GB before dying (for comparison MML estimate with GPstuff takes 45s, and less than 1GB memory)). Comaprison to MML with GPstuff is not fair, but I was still surprised that Stan for GP is so slow and that running out of memory with 1000 data points. We have had discussion on things which could make GPs faster in Stan. Feel free to use this example for testing (sorry for not including R code, and I guess the Matlab code would not be so useful for you).

I played with GP models in Stan a bit about a year ago (though with regression instead of classification).  The one major thing that is likely slowing this down is the call to cholesky_decompose which, for a matrix of even modest size, will be painfully slow.  Have you tried writing the model with f as the unknown and f ~ multi_normal(0,C) instead of z ~ normal(0,1)?  I suspect that this will make evaluating and differentiating the log likelihood much faster, though it may make curvature worse for sampling.

Cheers,

Hey Aki, can you send the matlab code? I was having out-of-memory
issues that were resolved when I just told Stan to only save a few
parameters of interest (rather than entire covariance matrices). Is
this option available in MatlabStan?

@Marcus: sure, cholesky_decompose can be slow, but what's happening

had not removed the costly linear algebra steps (i.e. calculate C at
each sampling step, calculate Cholesky). To me this suggests that the
curvature was bad for sampling, but maybe I'm not thinking about this
correctly. Anyone have intuition about that?

metric) for HMC? When I was last trying to debug this I found some
chains that ran really quickly while others took forever (on the same
data) and the mass matrix that was learned for each was pretty
different. Not sure the chains that ran fast were actually giving good
answers, but at least they ran. I feel like there should be some
connection between the mass matrix and the covariance C, but I went to
look in the literature to see if anyone had explored this (e.g.
Radford Neal didn't say much about what mass matrix he used in the
original HMC + GP work) and didn't find anything.

Seth

messages.author: 743bbacc59f4b25f
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] GP experiment
parts:
On Tuesday, February 24, 2015 at 11:07:25 PM UTC-5, Seth Flaxman wrote:
@Marcus: sure, cholesky_decompose can be slow, but what's happening
under the hood with multi_normal? There's no way around inverting the
matrix C and calculating its log-determinant, right? (And this is
often done with Cholesky...)

For a fixed precision matrix, it can avoid calculating the determinant and then the kernel of the multivariate normal is just a quadratic form, which Marcus has optimized a lot. And even if you input a fixed covariance matrix, I think it caches the Cholesky factorization, so the speed hit might be less noticeable.

For an unknown covariance matrix, there is not much in Stan now to avoid brute forcing a Cholesky factorization in vars. A lot of precision matrices in situations like this have the property that many of the off-diagonal elements approach zero. So, it might be possible to parameterize a precision matrix where those off-diagonal elements that approach zero are actually truncated to zero and then we might be able to utilize sparse algorithms. Another possibility is to parameterize the Cholesky factor of the covariance matrix, which would obviate the need to do a Cholesky decomposition of a covariance matrix. I haven't really looked into this either, but the first column of a Cholesky factor is a simple function of the first column of the covariance matrix it corresponds to. So, if you set the first column of the Cholesky factor according to the covariance function you have chosen, possibly the remaining below-diagonal elements of the Cholesky factor would fall into line conditional on that even if they were just unrestricted. You probably would have to do something clever about the diagonal elements of the Cholesky factor though.

There is an issue on GitHub for initializing the mass matrix, but I don't think it has been implemented yet.

Ben

> When I was debugging something like this, one thing I was surprised by

> had not removed the costly linear algebra steps (i.e. calculate C at
> each sampling step, calculate Cholesky). To me this suggests that the
> curvature was bad for sampling, but maybe I'm not thinking about this
> correctly. Anyone have intuition about that?

GP likelihoods as a function of the hyperparameters are notoriously nasty,
with lots of saddle points that make optimization (and sampling) hard.
I think this is particularly bad when trying to do ARD with a squared-
exponential kernel. Hyperpriors are critical here.

> Is there any support yet for initializing the mass matrix (aka the
> metric) for HMC? When I was last trying to debug this I found some
> chains that ran really quickly while others took forever (on the same
> data) and the mass matrix that was learned for each was pretty
> different. Not sure the chains that ran fast were actually giving good
> answers, but at least they ran.

My guess is that this is a manifestation of the nasty likelihood geometry
(different initializations lead to chains exploring different local
neighborhoods).
"Not sure the chains that ran fast were actually giving good

answers, but at least they ran.” This is a great way to upset anyone
who takes MCMC seriously. I jest, but in all seriousness slow but
diagnostic of pathologies is infinitely better than fast and ignorant.

> I feel like there should be some
> connection between the mass matrix and the covariance C, but I went to
> look in the literature to see if anyone had explored this (e.g.
> Radford Neal didn't say much about what mass matrix he used in the
> original HMC + GP work) and didn't find anything.

Nope, there’s no immediate connection. The GP covariance defines
the correlation of points in data space, not the hyperparameters space
from which we sample.

messages.author: 2a7f346506a3e9ff
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] GP experiment
parts:
The reason why cholesky_decompose is a lot slower than you think (vs multi_normal) has to do with the way autodiff works.  Basically, the slowest part of evaluating the log probability with Stan is creating autodiff variables.  A new one has to be created for every "elementary" operation that is performed on a parameter.  For instance, this is the reason that vectorization is such a big win, not because there can be fancy SIMD instructions under the hood, but because there are far fewer autodiff variables created.  This is also a big part of the reason that fixing the hyperparameters makes it much faster, because then the kernel matrix is no longer a parameter and doesn't need to be autodiff'd.

cholesky_decompose is particularly slow because it is literally autodiffing through all the operations of a cholesky decomposition.  This results in a MASSIVE number of autodiff variables (O(N^3) for an NxN covariance matrix) being created which takes far longer than just the basic Cholesky factorization of the underlying matrix.  In contrast, multi_normal has been fairly heavily optimized and specialized such that evaluating it creates only O(N) autodiff variables.  If someone was motivated, they could even bring that down to O(1).

So, in short, yes, multi_normal uses the Cholesky decomposition under the hood, but it does so in a far more efficient way than cholesky_decompose() is (or likely ever will be) able to.

Anyway, hope this helps clarify things a bit.  It's possible that the improved curvature behaviour of the Matt trick improves sampling enough that the speed gains of using multi_normal aren't worth it or are a wash, but I somewhat doubt it.

Cheers,
Marcus

There are two things that I can imagine happening here.  One, the curvature of the problem may be hard; given the nature of the model it could have a funnel like structure.  (it's not exactly that because the funnel would be distorted by the   RMHMC could help us here if it was ready but alas...

The other possibility, which the variability between chains somewhat suggests, is that the random initialization is performing really badly here.  Providing a well constructed initialization may help a lot and get you the best of both worlds.  For instance, randomly draw the kernel parameters (s_sexp, l_sexp, s_linear, s_constant), evaluate the kernel matrix C and then draw f ~ multi_normal(0,C) to construct the initialization.

This a case where having an initialization block (something we've talked about) would help a LOT so that you wouldn't have to reimplement your kernel functions outside the Stan model to produce the initialization.  An init block for a model like this would be maybe three lines of code...if we had support for that.

Cheers,
Marcus

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] GP experiment
parts:
Seth asked in email, but I'll answer here
> Hey Aki, you have HMC in GPStuff, right? How's it compare on this or
> other examples? And are there any important differences between your
> implementation and what Stan's doing?
>
> Any theories about why the samples from the model without Cholesky are
> so terrible?

When using HMC or NUTS in GPstuff, the sampling is made alternating the sampling of the latent values given the covariance function and likelihood parameters and the sampling of the covariance function and likelihood parameters given the latent values. The sampling of the latent values uses an approximative posterior covariance to create a transformed latent space (corresponding to using a mass matrix). This approximative posterior covariance combines the prior covariance and an approximative likelihood contribution. This transformation makes a big difference in the sampling efficiency. Since the transformation is conditional on the fixed covariance function and likelihood parameters, the transformation is fixed during the latent value sampling, and thus there is no need to compute the gradients through the Cholesky. Both these conditional samplings are fast, but the dependency between latent values and the covariance function and likelihood parameters makes the overall mixing slow, but not as slow as Stan without Cholesky. Without Cholesky there are really strong dependencies between latent values and a funnel when combined with sampling of the covariance function parameters at the same time. With Cholesky the sampling in Stan is efficient, it's just that computation of Cholesky and autodiffing through Cholesky makes it slow and use a lot of memory as Marcus explained.

Recently, instead of HMC/NUTS I've used combination of elliptical slice sampler and surrogate slice sampler (which samples both the latent values and the covariance function and likelihood parameters at the same time with a GP specific algorithm), which seems to produce better overall mixing speed.

Sampling for GP models has been studied a lot, and based on all that and my own experiments, I think that HMC/NUTS/RHMC is not going to be fast for sampling both latent values and the covariance function and likelihood parameters. These recent Stan experiments seem to provide additional evidence for that.

To get fast GPs in Stan, the integration over the latent values should be made using Laplace's method (or EP).

Aki
